name: SELECT
desc: Chooses the columns the query returns. List them instead of using *, so the JSON shape matches the frontend.
body:
The clause order you write is not the order MySQL runs. `FROM` and the joins build rows, `WHERE` filters them, `GROUP BY` folds them, `HAVING` filters groups, then `SELECT` computes the output. A `SELECT` alias therefore works in `ORDER BY` and fails in `WHERE`.

`SELECT *` sends every column, including ones the page has no slot for, and it breaks quietly when a column is added. Name the columns.

name: WHERE
desc: Keeps only the rows where the condition is true. Runs before grouping, so it can use columns but not COUNT or SUM.

name: AND / OR
syntax: WHERE cond1 AND cond2 | WHERE cond1 OR cond2
desc: AND binds tighter than OR. Parenthesise the group you mean, or the query filters something else.

name: IN ()
desc: Matches any value in the list. Shorter than a chain of ORs and easier to build from a filter array.
example:
-- Three named cities
SELECT id, name, city FROM hotels
WHERE city IN ('Budapest', 'Debrecen', 'Eger');

-- NOT IN is unsafe when the subquery can return NULL: one NULL
-- makes every comparison unknown and the result empty.
SELECT id, name FROM hotels
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT hotel_id FROM bookings WHERE hotel_id IS NOT NULL);

name: BETWEEN
syntax: WHERE column BETWEEN low AND high
desc: Inclusive range, both ends included. Works on numbers and on dates in YYYY-MM-DD form.

name: LIKE
desc: Pattern match where % means any run of characters and _ means exactly one. The exam search box is built on it.
example:
-- Contains "view", case insensitive on this schema
SELECT id, name FROM hotels WHERE name LIKE '%view%';

-- Search across two tables. The pattern is bound, not concatenated.
SELECT b.customer_email, c.first_name, h.name
FROM bookings b
JOIN customers c ON c.email = b.customer_email
JOIN hotels h    ON h.id = b.hotel_id
WHERE c.first_name LIKE CONCAT('%', ?, '%')
   OR c.last_name  LIKE CONCAT('%', ?, '%')
   OR h.name       LIKE CONCAT('%', ?, '%');

name: ORDER BY
desc: Sorts the result. Reads keys left to right, ASC by default. Add a unique tiebreaker when the sort key repeats.
example:
-- Highest stars first, names A to Z inside equal stars
SELECT id, name, stars FROM hotels
ORDER BY stars DESC, name ASC, id ASC;

-- Sort by an expression: longest stay first
SELECT customer_email, hotel_id,
       DATEDIFF(end_date, start_date) AS nights
FROM bookings
ORDER BY nights DESC, start_date ASC;

name: LIMIT / OFFSET
desc: Cuts the result to count rows after sorting. Without ORDER BY the rows are arbitrary, not the first ones.
example:
-- Page 3 of a ten row list, with a stable tiebreaker
SELECT id, name, city FROM hotels
ORDER BY name, id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

-- Longest booking, exactly one row
SELECT customer_email, hotel_id, start_date, end_date
FROM bookings
ORDER BY DATEDIFF(end_date, start_date) DESC, start_date ASC
LIMIT 1;
body: In a route, a limit from `req.query` arrives as a string. `pool.query` quotes it into `LIMIT '10'` and MySQL rejects the syntax. Either use `pool.execute` and bind `?`, or parse it to a positive integer, cap it, and inline the number.

name: JOIN
syntax: FROM a JOIN b ON b.key = a.key
desc: Inner join: keeps only the rows that find a partner on the other side. JOIN alone means INNER JOIN.
example:
-- Every hotel with its owner's name
SELECT h.id, h.name, h.city, c.first_name, c.last_name
FROM hotels h
JOIN customers c ON c.email = h.owner_email
ORDER BY h.name, h.id;

-- A booking needs two joins: the guest and the hotel
SELECT b.customer_email, c.last_name, h.name AS hotel_name, b.start_date
FROM bookings b
JOIN customers c ON c.email = b.customer_email
JOIN hotels h    ON h.id = b.hotel_id;

name: LEFT JOIN
syntax: FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.key = a.key
desc: Keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULL where nothing matches. Use it when a zero must still appear.
example:
-- Every hotel, with the number of bookings. COUNT(column)
-- skips NULL, so a hotel with none counts 0.
SELECT h.id, h.name, COUNT(b.customer_email) AS bookings
FROM hotels h
LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.hotel_id = h.id
GROUP BY h.id, h.name
ORDER BY bookings DESC, h.name;
body:
A filter on the right table in `WHERE` turns the outer join back into an inner one, because `NULL >= '2025-01-01'` is unknown. Put that condition in `ON`:

```sql
SELECT h.id, h.name, b.start_date
FROM hotels h
LEFT JOIN bookings b
       ON b.hotel_id = h.id
      AND b.start_date >= '2025-01-01'
      AND b.start_date <  '2026-01-01';
```

Also, `COUNT(*)` would count the NULL padded row and report 1 booking for a hotel with none. Count a column from the right table instead.

name: GROUP BY
syntax: SELECT key, AGG(...) FROM table GROUP BY key
desc: Folds rows that share values into one row per group. Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
example:
-- Hotels per city, with the average star rating
SELECT city,
       COUNT(*) AS hotels,
       AVG(stars) AS avg_stars
FROM hotels
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY hotels DESC, city;

-- Yearly booking counts from the start date
SELECT YEAR(start_date) AS booking_year, COUNT(*) AS bookings
FROM bookings
GROUP BY YEAR(start_date)
ORDER BY booking_year;

name: HAVING
desc: Filters groups after the aggregates are computed. The only place to put a condition on COUNT, SUM or AVG.
example:
-- Cities that own more than one hotel
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS hotels
FROM hotels
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY city;

-- Row filter in WHERE, group filter in HAVING
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS four_star
FROM hotels
WHERE stars = 4
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

name: COUNT()
desc: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(column) skips NULLs, COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts different non-null values.
example:
-- Rows, distinct guests, and guests with a phone
SELECT COUNT(*)                  AS bookings,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_email) AS guests
FROM bookings;

-- With a left join, count the right table column so zero stays zero
SELECT h.name, COUNT(b.customer_email) AS bookings
FROM hotels h
LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.hotel_id = h.id
GROUP BY h.id, h.name;

name: SUM() / AVG()
desc: Adds or averages the non-null values of a group. Returns NULL when no row qualifies, so wrap totals in COALESCE.
example:
-- Guest totals for the whole table: one row, zero when empty
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(adults), 0)   AS adults,
       COALESCE(SUM(children), 0) AS children,
       COALESCE(SUM(adults + children + boylovers), 0) AS guests
FROM bookings;

-- Average stars per city, ignoring cities with no row
SELECT city, ROUND(AVG(stars), 2) AS avg_stars
FROM hotels
GROUP BY city;

name: COALESCE()
desc: Returns the first argument that is not NULL. Converts a NULL total into 0 and keeps a partial UPDATE from erasing a column.
example:
-- JSON gets 0, not null, when nothing matches
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(adults), 0) AS adults FROM bookings
WHERE start_date <= '2025-07-31' AND end_date >= '2025-07-01';

-- Keep the old value when the new one is NULL
UPDATE bookings
SET adults = COALESCE(?, adults),
    children = COALESCE(?, children)
WHERE customer_email = ? AND hotel_id = ?;

name: INSERT INTO
desc: Adds rows. Always name the columns, and bind the values from Node with placeholders.

name: UPDATE
syntax: UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition
desc: Changes the matched rows. Without WHERE it changes every row, so run the condition as a SELECT first.
example:
-- Change one booking. The key is the pair, so the WHERE has both.
UPDATE bookings
SET start_date = '2025-09-02',
    end_date   = '2025-09-04',
    adults     = 3
WHERE customer_email = 'dora.toth@example.com'
  AND hotel_id = 1;

-- Count what the WHERE matches before the write
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bookings WHERE hotel_id = 1;

name: DELETE
desc: Removes the matched rows and returns affectedRows. Deleting a parent row may cascade or be refused by a foreign key.
example:
-- One booking, addressed by the composite key
DELETE FROM bookings
WHERE customer_email = 'dora.toth@example.com'
  AND hotel_id = 1;

-- A guest is removed together with their bookings (ON DELETE CASCADE),
-- but a guest who owns a hotel is refused (ON DELETE RESTRICT)
DELETE FROM customers WHERE email = 'dora.toth@example.com';

name: START TRANSACTION
desc: Groups statements so they all land or none do. In Node the whole transaction must run on one pooled connection.

name: date range overlap
desc: Selects rows whose date range touches the requested period. Both comparisons are needed; either one alone is wrong.
example:
-- Stays that touch July 2025. A stay ending on the 1st is included,
-- and so is one starting on the 31st.
SELECT customer_email, hotel_id, start_date, end_date
FROM bookings
WHERE start_date <= '2025-07-31'
  AND end_date   >= '2025-07-01';

-- Guest totals for the same period, one row back
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(adults), 0)   AS adults,
       COALESCE(SUM(children), 0) AS children
FROM bookings
WHERE start_date <= ? AND end_date >= ?;
body: The strict form, for "which room is free for the night of the 10th", uses `start_date <= date AND end_date > date`, because a guest who checks out on the 10th frees the room. Pick one rule, write it in a comment, and test the boundary where a stay ends exactly on the arrival date.

name: DATEDIFF() / YEAR()
desc: Whole days from the second date to the first. DATEDIFF(end_date, start_date) is the number of nights in a booking.
example:
-- Nights per booking, longest first
SELECT customer_email, hotel_id, start_date, end_date,
       DATEDIFF(end_date, start_date) AS nights
FROM bookings
ORDER BY nights DESC, start_date ASC;

-- Calendar parts and a month label
SELECT YEAR(start_date) AS y, MONTH(start_date) AS m,
       DATE_FORMAT(start_date, '%Y-%m') AS month_label
FROM bookings;

SELECT CURDATE();                              -- today
SELECT DATE_ADD('2025-07-01', INTERVAL 7 DAY);  -- 2025-07-08

name: CREATE INDEX
syntax: CREATE INDEX name ON table (column[, column2])
desc: Speeds up filters, joins and sorts on the indexed columns. Costs space and a little write time on every insert.

name: EXPLAIN
desc: Prints the query plan instead of running the query. Check type and rows to see whether an index did the work.
example:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM bookings WHERE hotel_id = 1;

-- type = ALL means a full table scan.
-- type = ref or range means an index was used.
-- key shows which index, rows estimates the work.

name: EXISTS / NOT EXISTS
desc: Tests whether the subquery returns at least one row. Stops at the first match and stays correct when NULLs are involved.
example:
-- Hotels that have at least one booking
SELECT h.id, h.name
FROM hotels h
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bookings b WHERE b.hotel_id = h.id);

-- Hotels with no booking at all. Safer than NOT IN, which breaks
-- when the subquery returns NULL.
SELECT h.id, h.name
FROM hotels h
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bookings b WHERE b.hotel_id = h.id);

name: ? placeholder
desc: Sends values separately from the statement so user text can never become SQL. The first step against injection.

name: result.insertId
desc: The result object of a write. insertId is the generated key, affectedRows the number of rows changed.

name: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
syntax: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE column = VALUES(column)
desc: Insert, or update the existing row when a primary or unique key collides. One statement instead of a check and a race.
example:
-- A guest books a hotel once: the key is (customer_email, hotel_id)
INSERT INTO bookings (customer_email, hotel_id, start_date, end_date, adults)
VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
    start_date = VALUES(start_date),
    end_date   = VALUES(end_date),
    adults     = VALUES(adults);

-- affectedRows: 1 inserted, 2 updated, 0 unchanged
